title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
description: Brute force to optimized: DFS with a depth map versus a queue-based BFS with a per-round size snapshot.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its node values (from left to right, level by level, top to bottom).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","A list of lists, each inner list holding one level's node values left to right"],["Goal","Use breadth-first search (BFS) with a queue, processing one full level at a time"],["Constraints","Up to 2000 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Level by level, top to bottom\"","Breadth-first search (BFS) using a queue is the natural fit, since BFS visits nodes in exactly this level-by-level order"]]}

blocks.text: BFS naturally processes nodes in level order if the queue is drained in discrete "rounds", one round per level: capture the current queue's size at the start of a round, process exactly that many nodes (collecting their values and enqueuing their children), and that round's collected values form one complete level.

blocks.title: Analogy: Announcing Names Floor by Floor in a Building Evacuation
blocks.text: Picture evacuating a building floor by floor, announcing everyone's name on the current floor completely before moving on to announce the next floor down, never mixing names from different floors together.

blocks.caption: BFS with a queue, processing one full level at a time before moving to the next

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A queue-based BFS visits nodes in level order overall, but by default does not separate them into distinct levels automatically.

Observation 2: Capturing the queue's CURRENT size at the start of each round, and processing exactly that many nodes before enqueuing any of their children, ensures the round corresponds to exactly one tree level.

Observation 3: Repeating this "process a fixed-size batch, then move to the next" pattern until the queue is empty naturally produces one list of values per level, in order.
This leads to a queue-based BFS where each iteration processes exactly the current queue length worth of nodes, forming one level's output list.
Use DFS instead, tracking each node's depth as it is visited, and group all node values by depth only AFTER the traversal completes.
Why the code is written this way

items: Grouping node values by depth via DFS implements level order indirectly.
This needs a separate map data structure and a post-processing step, while BFS naturally produces the levels directly during traversal, with no extra bookkeeping.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the depth map plus recursion depth.
Limitation: BFS with a queue produces the levels directly and in order, without needing a separate grouping map.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Start a queue containing just the root (if not null). While the queue is non-empty: record its current size as the number of nodes in THIS level. Process exactly that many nodes: dequeue each, record its value into the current level's list, and enqueue its non-null children. After processing that many nodes, the current level's list is complete; append it to the result and move to the next round.
Use a queue-based BFS, processing exactly the current queue size worth of nodes per round to isolate each level.

Snapshotting the queue's size at the very start of each round, before any children are enqueued in that same round, guarantees that processing exactly that many dequeues consumes exactly one level's worth of nodes, correctly separating levels without any extra bookkeeping, while a plain queue-based BFS already guarantees left-to-right order within each level.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the queue and result, in the worst case (a wide, shallow tree).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["DFS with a depth map, grouped afterward","O(n)","O(n)","Correct, but indirect and needs post-processing."],["BFS with a queue, snapshot per round","O(n)","O(n)","The expected, natural solution."]]}

blocks.text: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal is the foundational BFS-on-trees problem: the "snapshot queue size per round" trick is the key technique for separating BFS output into discrete levels.

items: Forgetting to snapshot the queue size BEFORE enqueuing any children in the current round, which would incorrectly mix levels together.
Not handling the empty tree (null root) case, which should simply return an empty list.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty tree","Returns an empty list."],["A completely skewed tree (every node has only one child)","Each level has exactly one node."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "snapshot the queue size at the start of each round to separate levels" is the single most important detail to communicate for this pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "level by level, top to bottom", think: BFS with a queue, snapshotting the queue size per round.

items: How would you modify this to alternate direction per level (a zigzag level order traversal)?
Binary Tree Right Side View and Zigzag Level Order Traversal, both build directly on this same round-based BFS technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches cost O(n) time and space; BFS with the snapshot-size trick is the direct, standard solution requiring no post-processing.

items: Pattern: BFS with a queue, using the "snapshot queue size per round" trick to separate levels.
Core Idea: process exactly the current queue size worth of nodes per round, before any of that round's children get enqueued.
Most Important Observation: snapshotting the queue size before enqueuing children is what correctly isolates each level.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy to medium BFS-on-trees problem.
One line memory trick: snapshot the queue size, then drain exactly that many.
